transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, honestly, I think I just hit a wall. What finally pushed me to come in is that I can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. I mean, between the patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines—my wife actually bought this beautiful piece for our anniversary last year from a gallery in Chelsea, which reminds me I still need to get it framed. I tried to do it myself, but you know how custom frames are, if you're off by even a fraction of an inch, the whole thing looks terrible. I used to build models when I was a kid, so you'd think I'd be good at that sort of precision work. But anyway, yeah, the team decisions at work, all these deadlines... I just end up starting whatever is loudest instead of what actually matters. It's like I'm constantly putting out fires, but I'm the one who accidentally started them because I was looking at something else.

You mentioned having trouble organizing tasks and focusing on what matters most. Does this happen mostly at work, or do you also notice it in other parts of your life, like at home or in social situations?

I'm not really sure if it's mostly at work... I mean, I guess it happens everywhere? I haven't really tracked it to see where it's worse. Like at home... well, just yesterday I was trying to figure out if we needed groceries, but then I noticed the fridge water filter light was on. And those filters are so ridiculously expensive if you buy the name brand, so I went on my laptop to find a generic one, which somehow led me down this massive rabbit hole about whole-house water filtration systems. 

Did you know that reverse osmosis actually strips out all the good minerals, too? You have to buy a special attachment to remineralize the water before you drink it. My brother-in-law lives out in Colorado and he gets his water straight from a well on his property, and it tastes incredible. We went to visit him last summer, drove the whole way. I absolutely hate flying these days, the airports are just a complete mess, and they always make you gate-check your carry-on anyway, so what's the point? We took the scenic route through Utah, which was beautiful, but... 

Wait, sorry, what were you asking? Oh, right, social situations. Uh... I don't know, I haven't really noticed anything specific there. What do you mean by that exactly?
Can you think of a time when you were deeply focused on something for a long period without getting distracted?

Deeply focused? Uh... honestly, I don't really know. I'm trying to think of the last time that happened. Maybe when I was a kid? But as an adult... I'm not sure. I mean, I can definitely get sucked into things, like that water filter research. Is that what you mean? Because I spent like three hours looking at plumbing schematics yesterday. 

Actually, speaking of plumbing, we had this massive leak in our basement a few years ago. The sump pump just completely gave out during this huge storm. We had to rip up all the carpet, and my wife was so upset because it was this vintage rug her grandmother gave us. We tried to get it professionally cleaned, but the guy said the water damage was just too extensive. He had this whole chemical process he explained to me, which was fascinating, actually. They use these massive industrial ozone generators to get the mildew smell out. I almost bought one on eBay just to have around, but they're apparently pretty dangerous if you don't know what you're doing. You can actually damage your lungs. 

But yeah, focused... I don't know. I guess I don't really have a good example of that. Unless the water filter thing counts?
Can you describe how you manage tasks that require sustained mental effort, like reading a report or following through on a project at work or home?

Sustained mental effort... right. Well, I try to just force myself to sit down and do it, you know? Like, I'll tell myself, "Okay, you're not getting up until this code review is done." I'm a software developer, by the way. But then I'll be looking at a block of code, and I'll notice a function that could be optimized. Not even part of what I'm supposed to be reviewing, just something nearby. And I'll start thinking about different ways to refactor it, maybe using a newer library we just got access to. 

We just switched to this new enterprise license for our development tools, and let me tell you, the migration was an absolute nightmare. The IT guys were working over the weekend, and they brought in pizza, but it was from that place down the street that always burns the crust. I don't understand how a pizza place stays in business if they can't even get the crust right. It's literally the foundation of the pizza! I actually started making my own pizza dough at home during the pandemic. Sourdough, of course. Everybody was doing sourdough, but I got really into the hydration percentages. You have to weigh everything in grams, which makes total sense, but my wife hates it because she prefers just using measuring cups. She says I make baking feel like a chemistry lab. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, reading reports and stuff. Yeah, honestly, I don't know how I manage it. I usually end up reading the same paragraph like five times because my eyes are moving but my brain is somewhere else entirely. I don't really have a good system for it, to be honest.

When you're trying to complete tasks that require focus, like at work or home, do you find the disorganization and distraction happens consistently, or are there times when you can manage these tasks without much trouble?

Consistently? Yeah, I'd say it's pretty constant. I mean, it's gotten to the point where it's actually starting to damage my reputation at work. I completely missed this major checkpoint for a patent filing we were doing. And then we had this architecture review that was supposed to be my big moment to shine, but I was so all over the place that the other teams are now questioning if I can even lead the larger project. 

Which really stings, you know? Because I've been at this company for eight years. I remember when we first moved into that office building, it was an old converted warehouse. They kept the exposed brick, which looks cool, but the insulation is terrible. In the winter, you practically have to wear a parka at your desk. I ended up buying this little space heater, one of those ceramic ones? But it kept tripping the breaker because the wiring in that place is ancient. The facilities guy, Dave—great guy, he actually plays bass in a jazz fusion band on the weekends—he had to come up and reset it like three times in one day. He told me that they found newspapers from 1920 stuffed in the walls when they were renovating. Can you imagine? People used to just use old newspapers as insulation. It's a miracle the whole place hasn't gone up in flames.

But, uh... yeah, the distractions. It's definitely causing real problems for me now, especially with that architecture review. I just couldn't keep my thoughts organized enough to explain the system flow.
Can you think of any situation, either at work or at home, where you were able to stay consistently organized and complete tasks without becoming distracted or losing focus?

Consistently organized? Um... I'm trying to think. Honestly, no, not really. It's just so easy for me to get pulled away. Like, if I'm coding and Slack pings, or even if just a browser tab flashes in the background, it's over. Or sometimes it's not even external! A visual idea will just pop into my head, and I'll completely lose the thread of what I was working on. I'll end up spending twenty minutes going down some completely unrelated design rabbit hole. 

Actually, speaking of design, I was looking at the UI for this new smart thermostat we just got for the house. The interface is so poorly thought out. You have to tap through three different menus just to set up a basic schedule. I was looking into the company that makes them, and they were actually bought out by this massive conglomerate last year. It's funny how that happens, right? A small startup makes a great product, gets acquired, and then the quality just completely tanks because the parent company forces them to use their proprietary software framework. I had a buddy who worked for a startup that got bought by Oracle, and he said the culture shift was just brutal. They went from having free lunches and unlimited PTO to having to track their hours in this archaic system from the 90s. 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, staying organized without getting distracted. Yeah, no, between the Slack messages and my own brain, it's pretty much impossible for me to stay on track for very long.
Looking back, were you already having trouble with focus or staying organized as a child, or did these difficulties mostly start in adulthood?

As a child? Yeah, looking back, this was definitely there in grade school, long before I was a teenager. I actually know this for a fact because I was just helping my parents clean out their attic a few months ago, and I found a whole box of my old report cards. 

They still live in the same house I grew up in, this classic mid-century split-level. The attic is an absolute nightmare to get into, though. You have to pull down these incredibly rickety wooden stairs from the ceiling, and my dad absolutely refuses to replace them. He's one of those guys who thinks if it isn't completely snapped in half, you don't fix it. I mean, he still uses a gas lawnmower from, like, 1995. He just keeps rebuilding the carburetor every spring. I tried to tell him he could get a battery-powered one now—they're so much quieter, no gas fumes, no maintenance—but he won't hear of it. He claims the electric ones don't have enough torque, which is actually a complete misconception because electric motors deliver instant torque, unlike combustion engines which have to reach a certain RPM before they peak... 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, my childhood. Yeah, the report cards. Basically, every single teacher wrote the exact same thing: they'd say I was a bright kid, but I daydreamed constantly. And I was always losing my homework folders. Or, the most frustrating part was, I would actually do the homework—like, I'd finish the entire assignment at my desk at home—and then just completely forget to turn it in the next day. So yeah, it's been happening since I was a little kid.
